activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Paisley ran to the circle rug at daycare. Miss Dana was holding her guitar.

"We need one more friend to sing," said Miss Dana. Ben sat in the corner. He was sad because his toy car was missing.

Paisley waved to him. "Come sing with us!" Ben came slowly and sat down.

Miss Dana played the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five." Everyone clapped on each number. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Paisley clapped loud on ten. Ben clapped too, just a little.

Then it was snack time. Miss Dana asked, "Who wants to pass out the cups?" Paisley raised her hand high.

She counted the cups as she set them out. "One, two, three." The cups made a little click on the table each time. "Four, five, six, seven, eight." Now everyone had a cup but Ben.

"Nine," said Paisley, putting one at his spot. Ben smiled.

At the art table, Paisley found a crayon with a sharp point. She used it to draw ten circles. "Look, Ben! I can count them!" She tapped each one. Ben laughed at her tapping joke and tapped some too.

Then he held up his drawing of a red car.

"Is that your toy car?" Paisley asked.

"Yes," said Ben. "I can make a new one."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Julia could not find her bear. She looked under the bed. She looked in the toy box. No bear. Julia felt sad. Her lip went down, down, down.

Then she heard a bump. It came from the laundry basket. Julia felt a little scared. She held her mama's shirt tight. "Mama, something is in there," she said.

Mama lifted the towel. Out popped bear! Julia felt so excited. She jumped up and clapped. "Bear!" she shouted. Then she felt angry too. "Bad bear! You hid from me!"

Bear's fur was warm and sweet, like sunshine. Julia gave him a big hug. She stuck him under her arm, where he fit just right. "Bedtime, bear," she said. She turned off the light switch with Mama's help. Julia felt happy now. She closed her eyes and whispered, "Sleep tight, little bear."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Jack walked home with Daddy. He held a small box. Inside was a bunny. Her name was Pip.

Pip was hungry. She bit the box. She made a funny hole.

"She needs food," said Daddy. They got a shiny spoon. Daddy put bunny food in Pip's bowl. Jack gave her a leaf of lettuce.

Pip ate the lettuce. Then she stopped biting. She sat down and got very still. Her ears went soft.

"Is she sad?" asked Jack.

Daddy put his hand near Pip. Pip hopped onto Jack's lap. She nuzzled his hand.

Pip was not sad. She was happy and full.

Jack stroked her soft fur. Pip closed her eyes. The birds began to sing outside.

Jack held her gently all the way home. "I will feed you every day," he said.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jacob wanted to find his brown ball. It had rolled into the backyard. He held Grandpa's hand and went out the door.

Grandpa was cooking at the grill. The grill was hot. It made sizzling sounds. "Stay here with me," Grandpa said. Jacob sat on the step, close to Grandpa.

Jacob saw something round near the fence. It was under a spiky bush. He stood up. "I see my ball!" he said. Jacob took one step toward the bush. Grandpa caught his hand fast. "Not there. The bush has sharp sticks. I will get it."

Grandpa got a long stick. He pushed the ball out with it. The ball rolled to Jacob's feet. Jacob picked it up. It was warm from sitting in the sun. His hands felt the warm. Then he touched the cold step. Cold!

"Can we share the ball?" Grandpa asked. Jacob rolled it to Grandpa. Grandpa rolled it back. They played until the food was done. Then they sat together and ate warm food at the little table.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Charles sat at the dinner table. He wanted the big red cup. It was the cup with paint on it, little blue stars painted by his sister May.

"Can I have the red cup?" asked Charles.

"You had it last night," said May. "Tonight it is my turn."

Charles looked at the plain white cup in front of him. He looked at the red cup. He reached out his hand.

Dad put his hand on top of Charles' hand. "One cup each," said Dad. "We all take a turn."

Charles frowned. Then he saw May sip from the red cup. She made a happy sound, a little "mm" sound.

"Is the red cup the best cup?" asked Charles.

"No," said May. "The milk tastes the same."

Charles picked up his white cup. He took a sip. The milk was cold and sweet. May was right. It tasted the same.

"Your turn tomorrow," said May. "I promise."

Charles smiled. "Okay. You can have my blue plate too."

"You want to share?" asked May.

"Yes. Fair is fair," said Charles.

Mom laughed. "Good sharing, Charles."

After dinner, Charles felt sleepy. The dog was asleep under the table. Charles patted his soft ears.

"Tomorrow," said Charles, "I get the red cup."

"Tomorrow," said May, and she laughed again.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Brooks was on the swim team this summer. Every Tuesday he went to the big pool. His team was called the Little Fish.

Brooks wore goggles. The goggles hid his eyes. "Ready, Little Fish!" said Coach Mia. Brooks held the wall. He kicked his legs fast. Splash, splash, kick, kick. The water went up and up. Then Brooks felt himself move! His fast kicks made the water fly, and the water pushed him forward. Splash, splash, kick, kick. He moved some more.

Brooks counted the wall marks. One, two, three. Then he touched the far wall. Coach Mia clapped. Brooks climbed out and wrapped up in his big white towel. It was soft and snowy like a cloud. He sat by the sheep float bobbing in the shallow end. "I kicked hard," Brooks said, "and I went fast!"

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Aiden put on his red boot. Then he put on the other one. "We need to go," said Mama. "The big meal is at the hall."

At the hall, everyone held hands. But Aiden did not know the words. "Say them with me," said Grandma. She squeezed his hand. Aiden squeezed back.

Grandma said the blessing. Aiden said it too, word by word. When he said the last word, everyone smiled. Then everyone picked up a fork. "The food waits for the words," said Grandma. "Is that true?" asked Aiden. "Watch," she said.

Aiden watched. No fork moved. Then Grandpa said, "Amen!" and every fork went down at once. The plates went clink, clink, clink.

Next month, Aiden ran in with one boot on. He held out his hands first. "Wait, wait!" he said. "The food needs the words!" Grandma laughed and laughed. "You say them, Aiden."

Aiden said the blessing all by himself.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Kayden wanted warm cookies. It was cold winter outside. Mom said, "Let's bake." Kayden helped from his chair. He had two eyes to see the flour. It looked white and soft like snow. He had two ears to hear the mixer. It went round and round. The dough got smooth.

Then Kayden had a problem. "How do I know when cookies are done?" he asked. Mom said, "Use your body. It knows." Kayden used one nose to smell. Mmm, sweet! The smell filled the kitchen. He waited. His nose smelled warm butter and sugar. "Done!" said Mom. She used the big oven mitt. Kayden touched a cooled cookie with one hand. It felt bumpy. He tasted it with his tongue. Sweet! "I will remember this," said Kayden. He counted his helpers: two eyes, two ears, one nose, one tongue, two hands. Mom laughed and ate one too.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Blake wanted to fill the big water table at daycare. She turned the small faucet on top. Only a little water came out.

"Try the big faucet," said her teacher, Ms. Ruiz. "The big one is fast. The small one is slow." Blake turned the big faucet. Whoosh! The water ran fast. Soon the table was full. "That was fast," said Blake. "The small faucet was slow."

Then Blake touched the water. "Brrr, it is cold," she said. Ms. Ruiz brought a kettle. "The water in here is hot. I will pour it. You watch." She poured a little hot water in. Blake touched the side of the table. "Now it is warm. Not too hot. Not too cold."

"Time to play," said Ms. Ruiz. Blake dropped in a big boat and a small duck. She pushed the boat. It went fast. The duck floated slow. "Talk like a duck, Daisy duck," said Blake. Daisy laughed and clapped.

"You did it all alone," said Ms. Ruiz. "Big and small. Hot and cold. Fast and slow." Blake pushed the boat again. The small duck bobbed behind it, all the way to the bottom of the table.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Theodore went to the library with his mama. He found a book about a spider. The spider had eight little eyes. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight," said Theodore. He counted every eye.

He opened the book. The front was the part with the spider. He turned a page. The spider spun a web. He turned another page. A fly fell in. "Mama, the words tell me what happens!" said Theodore. His mama smiled.

Theodore wanted to keep the book forever. He hid it under his coat. A kind librarian knelt down beside him. "You can take it home," she said softly. "One, two, three weeks, then bring it back." Theodore gave back the book at the desk. He got a stamp on his hand. Then he picked out one more book, all by himself.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story: Clara saw her friend Ben cry at school. His face turned down. Clara made the same face. Then she felt sad too. Her teacher, Miss Kim, gave Ben a purple truck. Ben smiled big. Clara made the same face. Now she felt happy too. Clara wanted to know why. She tried it again at play time. Mia ran fast and looked excited. Clara made the same face. Her tummy felt jumpy. Then Sam fell down and looked scared. Clara made the same face. Her eyes got wide. Faces were like a magnet, Clara thought. One face pulled another face to it. She went to Sam and held his hand. "You are okay," she said. Sam stood up. His scared face went away. Clara's went away too. Then Miss Kim put music on. Everyone danced. Ben filled his truck with blocks and laughed. "You laugh, I laugh," said Clara. Sam laughed with her.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Sofia stood in the school hallway. She held her red backpack with both hands. Her backpack had a sheep on it, a soft white sheep with a bell. The big classroom door would not open. Sofia pushed it. Nothing happened. She pulled it. Nothing happened. "How do doors like this open?" she wondered.

Then she saw a small round button. It was red, like her backpack. Sofia pressed the button with one finger. Whoosh! The door slid open all by itself. Sofia's eyes went wide. She stepped back, and the door slid shut again. She pressed the button once more. Whoosh! The door opened again. "The button makes the door move," she whispered.

Inside, a teacher was mixing paint at a little table. Yellow paint went in. Blue paint went in. The teacher stirred and stirred. Now the paint was green! Sofia hung her backpack on a low hook and walked closer to watch. "Can I mix too?" she asked. The teacher gave her a stick and a small cup.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
John sat in his car seat. He was going to see Grandma. She had a big dog named Max. Max was hungry and had no bone.
The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small street. The sun was hot on the window. John rolled it up. The air inside turned cold.
A big truck went by. It was bigger than ten cars. A small bug sat on the glass. It was smaller than John's thumb.
At last they got to Grandma's house. Dad turned the car off. Grandma held a clean bowl of water. She gave Max a big bone. Max wagged his tail.
"Max was so hungry," said Grandma.
Max put his soft head on John's lap.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Maya ran into the garage. Dad had a big surprise there. It was a drum, red and shiny. Maya wanted to play it fast.

She tapped with one finger. The drum made a tiny sound. Tap. Tap. So small!

Then Dad put a drumstick in her hand. "Try this," he said. Maya hit the drum with the stick. BOOM! The drum made a big, big sound! Maya jumped. "Again!" she said. BOOM! BOOM! The whole garage rumbled. Her hair even wiggled.

The stick made the big sound. Her finger made the small sound. Maya tapped her finger again. Tap. Then she used the stick. BOOM! Tap. BOOM! She kept going back and forth.

"Listen, Dad!" she shouted. "I can make it big! I can make it small!" Dad laughed and covered his ears. Maya hit the drum one more time. BOOM!

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Zayn ran onto the big field at the community center. One coach, one whistle, one bouncy ball. "Time for soccer, Zayn!" Zayn kicked the ball with his red shoe. The ball went far. Then it stopped. Why did it stop? Zayn looked down. The grass was wet from the morning rain. He touched it with his hand. Cold! Wet and cold, like a splash.

Zayn tried again. On the dry grass, the ball rolled fast. On the wet grass, the ball went slow. He tried once more. Slow again on the wet part. Hmm. So that was it. Wet grass made the ball slow down.

His teammate Sam came running. Sam slipped and took a big fall. "The grass is slippery!" said Sam. Zayn waved to Coach Maya. "Watch this part," he said. He kicked the ball on the dry grass. It rolled and rolled, all the way to the net.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
William was on the swim team. Every Saturday morning he went to the big pool. His team was called the Blue Fish. William could not swim the whole lap yet.

Coach Maya said, "Kick your legs, William." William kicked hard. He splashed a lot. But he stayed in one spot. The water was cool and tickly. William felt stuck.

Then William watched his friend Mia. Mia kicked small kicks. Her legs went up and down, up and down. Mia moved fast through the water. William looked and looked.

William tried small kicks too. He kicked like Mia. Up and down, up and down. His body slid forward in the water. He moved past the rope. He moved all the way to the wall!

"Coach, look!" William called. Coach Maya clapped. Mia swam over and gave him a high five. "Good kicking," she said. William smiled big.

At the end, the team sat on the steps. Coach Maya handed out juice. William took two cups. He gave one to Mia. "Thank you," said Mia. William took a big sip of his juice and said, "Same time next Saturday?"

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Lily stood in the reading corner. She had a brand new library card. It was red with her name on it.

"I want this one," said Lily. She held up a book about fire trucks. The cover was rough like sandpaper.

"Good choice," said the librarian, Miss Jo. She stamped the card. Then she stamped a little paper in the book.

"What is that?" asked Lily.

"That paper tells you the day the book comes back," said Miss Jo. "Then other kids can read it too."

Lily frowned. "But I want to keep it forever."

Miss Jo smiled. "You can borrow it again later."

Lily took the book home. She read it six times. She read it to her bear. She read it to her socks.

At bedtime, Mom said, "We can hang your new library card on the wall by your bed."

"Okay," said Lily. "But the book goes back on Sunday. My friend Ben wants the fire trucks next."

On Sunday, Lily carried the book all by herself. She set it on the desk, nice and flat.

"Here," she said. "But can I borrow it again?"

"You sure can," said Miss Jo. She stamped the book once more.

Lily grinned. "Ben, don't bend the rough cover," she whispered. "I need it back."

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ethan wanted the red crayon. It sat high on the art shelf. His paint dragon needed red fire, and the red crayon was the magic fire holder.

Ethan jumped. His hand could not reach. He tried a big stretch. Still no crayon. He almost pushed a chair over to climb. His teacher, Miss Amy, came fast. "No climbing, Ethan," she said. "Ask me for help instead."

"Miss Amy, please get the red crayon?" Ethan asked. Miss Amy smiled. She took it down with one gentle hand. "Thank you," said Ethan. He ran back to his dragon.

Then Ethan bumped the table. Lily's paint cup tipped. Blue paint ran across her paper cat. Lily began to cry. "Sorry, Lily," said Ethan. He grabbed a paper towel. Together they wiped the blue away.

The paint made a big blue lake. Lily laughed. "Now my cat can swim," she said. Ethan drew red fire over the lake. The dragon flew above it. "Roar," said Ethan. "Thank you for my lake," said Lily.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Colton ran to the snack table at daycare. His eyes saw a big orange basket. Teacher Mia lifted the lid. "Guess what is inside," she said.

Colton used his nose to sniff. "I smell apples!" he said. It was true. A pile of red apples sat in the basket. Everyone clapped.

Teacher Mia gave each friend one apple slice. Colton touched his slice. It felt cool and smooth. He took a big bite. His tongue tasted sweet apple juice. Yum!

Then Colton heard a loud crunch. He looked over. His friend Zoe was biting her apple. Crunch, crunch! Colton bit his apple too. His bite made a big crunch as well. The two friends crunched back and forth. Crunch! Crunch! Crunch!

Zoe laughed so hard that apple bits fell on her shirt. "You are messy," Colton said. He looked down at his own shirt. His shirt was messy too. Teacher Mia helped them wipe off the apple bits.

Then Colton held up his last piece of apple. He waved it in the air. "One more big crunch!" he said.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
It was Ellie's birthday. Everyone came to her classroom. Mama hung three balloons by the window. One balloon had a big owl on it. Ellie's friend Sam pointed. "The owl is upside down!" The owl balloon looked silly with its feet in the air.

Then the owl balloon came loose. It floated up and up. It was lost near the ceiling. Ellie could not reach it. Grandpa got a chair. He stood on the chair. He caught the owl. Now the owl hung right again, with its feet down. "Hoot hoot!" said Sam, and everyone laughed.

Next came the cake. Miss Tara, the teacher, lit three little candles. One candle, two candles, three candles. "Make a wish," said Mama. Ellie took a big breath. She blew and blew. One candle went out. Two candles went out. Three candles went out. "Again!" said Sam. "Not yet," laughed Miss Tara. "First we eat the cake."

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Lucy went to the park with her dad. She saw a red balloon tied to a bench. A boy stood near the bench. He was crying.

"Are you sad?" Lucy asked. The boy nodded. His balloon had a small hole. It got small and small. Soon it was just a flat piece of rubber.

Lucy had chalk in her bag. She took out the yellow one. "I can color you a balloon," she said. She drew a big yellow circle on the ground. She drew a string on it too.

The boy stopped crying. He looked at the yellow circle. "A balloon that never pops!" he said. Now he was happy.

A big dog ran by. It was loud. Lucy felt scared. She held her dad's hand. The dog's owner called it back. The dog sat down and wagged its tail.

Lucy patted the soft dog. "Nice dog," she said. The boy patted it too. The dog licked the chalk circle. It left a wet mark that looked like a smile.

"I want to draw more," said the boy. Lucy gave him the blue chalk. He drew a blue balloon next to the yellow one. Then he drew a green one. Lucy clapped her hands. She was so excited.

A girl came by with a ball. She grabbed the blue chalk without asking. Lucy felt angry. Her face went hot. "That's his chalk," she said.

The girl gave it back. "Sorry," she said. "Can I draw too?" The boy said yes. She drew a pink balloon with a bow.

Four balloons sat on the ground, all in a row. Lucy squinted one eye and looked at them. They seemed to shine in the sun.

The boy looked at his flat red balloon. Then he looked at the four chalk balloons. He smiled a big smile. "These are better," he said. "They can't fly away, and they can't pop."

Lucy drew one more thing. She drew a small hand holding a small hand. "That's us," she said. "Friends at the park."

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Everly sat in the big red seat. Mama sat next to her. A lady on stage held a violin. The lady played a song, and the song had a beat.

Everly wanted to clap too. She clapped fast, fast, fast. Her claps did not match the song at all. The boy next to her covered his ears. Everly put her hands in her lap.

Mama leaned close. "Try one clap, then wait," she said. "Then one more." Everly watched Mama's hands. Mama clapped, then waited, then clapped. It looked like a slow game. Everly watched and watched. Then she tried.

Clap, wait, clap, wait. Now her claps sat right on the beat. The song and her hands went together. The boy uncovered his ears and clapped too. Everly smiled so big her cheeks felt salty from the snack she had eaten before.

At the end, the violin got quiet. Everly stood up and sang her whole rhyme from memory. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." She did not miss one word. The lady on stage looked at Everly and clapped for her. Everly clapped back, clap, wait, clap.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Nathan sat at the big table in writing club. He had a new hat on. It was too wide and slid over his eyes. He pushed it back.

Nathan wanted to write his name. He held the pencil in his whole fist. He made a line. The line sank down into a squiggle. It did not look like a letter at all.

The teacher, Miss Ada, sat next to him. "Do you want to try my way?" she asked. "Yes," said Nathan. She showed him how to pinch the pencil with two fingers. Nathan tried it. He made a tall N. Then an A. Then a T. "NAT!" he said. "That is me!"

Miss Ada clapped. Then Nathan saw a small H at the end of her card. He copied it. Now the card said NATH. Nathan laughed. "One more letter tomorrow," said Miss Ada. Nathan drew a wide smiley face next to his name.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Margot sat on the couch with Daddy. The big game was on TV. Everyone wore red shirts.

"Go, go, go!" they all shouted. Margot shouted too. "Go, go, go!"

Then baby Sam began to cry. The shouting was too loud for him. Aunt Jen picked Sam up. "He needs it quiet," she said.

Margot wanted Sam to feel better. She tried something. She clapped her hands very softly. Sam stopped crying. He looked at her leg, kicking slow and lazy on the couch. He made a little smile.

"Does he like soft claps?" Margot asked. "Yes, he does," said Aunt Jen.

So Margot clapped softly again. Sam smiled bigger. Now when the game got loud, Margot did not hurry to shout. She clapped her soft clap, just for Sam, and he giggled.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Jordan dug a small hole with his hands. His teacher, Miss Ana, made the holes deep enough for seeds. Jordan dropped a carrot seed in each one. Then he patted the soil down, soft and flat.

Every day Jordan ran to the garden circle. He watered the dirt with a little blue can. But nothing came up. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. Miss Ana smiled. "Seeds need water every day," she said. Jordan saw that his friend Mia had forgotten to water her spot. Mia's dirt was dry and cracked. Jordan shared his water can with her.

Soon little green leaves popped up. Jordan's leaves came first. Then Mia's leaves came too, right after Jordan gave her water. Jordan clapped his hands. "Look, Mia! Water makes them grow!" Mia laughed and filled the can again.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Ethan had a library book about a dog. It was time for bed. He held the book tight. "I want to keep this book forever," he said.

Dad sat on the bed. "Time to read," he said. "Open the front cover. That is where we start." Ethan turned the pages one by one. He saw the dog bark at a cat. Then the cat ran up a tree.

Ethan pointed at the letters. "What do these say?" he asked. Dad read the words out loud. Ethan looked at the page. The words told about the dog. The words and the picture went together.

At the last page, Ethan frowned. "Can we read it again?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "But on Friday we take the book back. Someone else wants to read it too." Ethan held the book to his chest. He was not sure.

On Friday, Ethan carried the book to the library. He set it on the desk. Then he saw a girl pick it up. She hugged it just like he had. Ethan waved at her. "The dog barks at a cat," he told her. She smiled and opened the front cover.

That night, Dad gave Ethan a new library book. It had a long, long train on the cover. Ethan opened the front page. "This one is mine for a while," he said. "But not forever." He patted the cover gently and turned the first page.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
William sat in his car seat. He was going to Grandma's house. "Are we there yet?" he asked.

Mom said, "Play a game. Look out the window." William looked. He saw a cow! Then he saw a sheep. Then a dog by a fence. "Animals!" he shouted. Mom laughed.

William reached into his bag. He wanted his red crayon. He wanted to draw the cow. But the crayon was missing! "Oh no," said William. He looked under his coat. He looked by his feet. No crayon.

Then he saw his toy truck on the seat. He pushed the truck. The truck rolled. The crayon rolled out from under the truck! "Found it!" said William. He picked it up. He drew a cow on his paper. He drew a sheep too.

"I'm hungry," said William. Mom gave him a banana. William ate it up. Then he drew a big yellow banana. Outside, a horse ran by. William drew the horse fast, fast, fast.

The car stopped. "We are here!" said Mom. William held up his paper. "Look, Grandma! Animals and foods!"

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Michael was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make a picture for her. Grandma put red paint, yellow paint, and a brush on the table. Michael dipped the brush in the red paint. He made a big red circle on the paper.

Then he wanted a sun too. Grandma said, "Try the yellow paint next." Michael put the brush in the yellow paint. He touched the yellow onto his red circle. The red circle turned orange! Michael looked and looked. His eyes got very big.

"Grandma, come see!" he said. Grandma came to the table. "What a pretty orange sun," she said. Michael made another circle. He put red, then yellow, and watched the orange grow again. "This one is for you," he said, and he held it up high.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday Grandma made cookies with Madelyn. They were warm and sweet. Today all the cookies were gone. Madelyn wanted more cookies now.

"Can we bake cookies today?" she asked.

"Mixing comes first," said Grandma. "Baking comes later."

Madelyn helped mix the dough. She dropped one spoon of dough onto the pan. Plop. Then she dropped another. Plop. Soon the pan was full.

Then the doorbell rang. It was the mail carrier with a letter. The letter was for Grandma. It was stuck a little in the door, and Grandma pulled it out. The letter was from Aunt Jo. It said, "I will visit tomorrow."

"Tomorrow," said Madelyn. "That is after today."

"That is right," said Grandma.

Grandma put the pan in the oven. Madelyn watched from her chair. The kitchen began to smell sweet. The dough puffed up into round cookies.

"Now we wait," said Grandma. "Waiting comes before eating."

Madelyn waited. She looked at the oven. She looked at the letter.

At last the cookies were ready. Grandma put one on a plate for Madelyn. It was warm and sweet, just like yesterday's.

"Tomorrow Aunt Jo can have one too," said Madelyn, and she took a big bite.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Hailey wanted to blow the bubbles. But her brother Sam had the wand. Sam blew one bubble. Then he blew two more.

"Next it is my turn," Hailey said. Sam gave her the wand. Hailey dipped it in the cup. She blew a big, round bubble. Sam smiled and clapped.

Then Hailey saw Sam's face go sad. He sat down on the step. Hailey looked at the wand in her hand. She held it out to Sam. "Your turn now," she said.

Sam took the wand. He blew a bubble that floated over the street. It popped in the air.

Mom called, "Snack time!" They ran inside. Two apple slices sat on each plate. Same for Hailey, same for Sam. They sat down side by side. Hailey took a big bite of her apple and smiled.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds the big blocks first. Big blocks go on the bottom. Then he finds the small blocks. Small blocks go on the top.

The tower grows tall. Carter pats each block. "Slow and steady," says his teacher, Miss Jo. Carter goes slow. One block. Then one more.

His friend Mia runs by fast. Her feet go stamp, stamp, stamp. The big tower wiggles. It falls down with a crash. All the blocks are on the floor now. They look dirty, so Miss Jo wipes them with a wet cloth.

Carter waits. He waits until Mia stops running. Then he starts again. Big blocks on the bottom. Small blocks on the top. Slow and steady. Slow and steady.

At snack time, Miss Jo brings warm muffins. "Hot, hot," she says, and blows on each one. Carter waits for his muffin to cool. He takes a small bite. Not hot anymore. Just right.

After snack, Carter builds his tower again. Nobody runs this time. The big tower stands tall. It does not wiggle. It does not fall.

"Look, Miss Jo!" says Carter. "My tower is so big!"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Blake wanted a big tomato of her own. She held a tiny plant in her hand. "This one is too little," she said. Dad smiled. "Watch what water does."

Blake put the plant in a pot. She patted the dirt down soft. Then she gave it water from a small can. The dirt turned dark and wet.

Every day Blake came back. She counted the leaves. The number got bigger and bigger. One, two, three, four! The little plant grew tall like her knees.

Then one morning Blake saw something red. A tomato! It was round and shiny. Dad picked it and washed it. Blake took a taste. "Yum," she said. "Water made it grow." Dad laughed. "And you helped."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Matteo wanted to see the snow again. Yesterday the snow had fallen. Today the snow was melting. Little pools of water sat on the path.

"Will it snow again?" Matteo asked. Mom smiled. "Later," she said. "First comes bedtime, then comes tomorrow."

Matteo looked out the window now. The sky was dark. The melting snow shone in the light. He could not see new snow yet.

Mom helped him put on his warm pajamas. He brushed his teeth. He picked a book about a bear. Mom read it in her soft voice.

Matteo's face felt sleepy. He yawned a big yawn. "Sleep now," Mom said. "Snow later."

He closed his eyes. He waited and waited. Then he fell fast asleep.

In the morning, the sun came up. Matteo ran to the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling again! It fell on the trees. It fell on the path. It covered the old melting snow.

"Mom! Mom!" Matteo called. "Tomorrow came! And the snow came too!" He pressed his warm hands on the cold glass. "Today it snows!"

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Harper went to the pharmacy with Dad. She saw a little bottle of soap. It had a duck on top. "Can I hold it?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Harper squeezed the duck. Soap came out. She squeezed again. More soap came out.

Then Harper saw a boy by the sink. He put soap on his hands. He rubbed and rubbed. He sang a song while he rubbed. "Why does he rub so long?" Harper asked. "Watch," said Dad. The boy held his hands under the water. The bubbles ran off. His hands came out shiny and clean.

Harper wanted shiny hands too. She put soap on her hands. "What if I rub quick?" she asked. "Try it," said Dad. She rubbed quick and rinsed. Her fingers still looked dull. "No shine!" she said. So she rubbed and rubbed. She sang the song too. The water carried the bubbles away. Harper held up her hands. They shined in the light. "Duck soap, you are my best friend," she said, and she squeezed the duck one more time.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Gabriel wanted to find something red at Grandma's house. He looked in the big kitchen drawer. He found a blue spoon. He looked under the little table. He found a yellow cup. He looked in the toy box. He found a green ball.

"Grandma, I can't find red," said Gabriel. Grandma smiled. "Come to the window," she said. Gabriel looked out. Grandma's red bike was leaning by the fence!

Then Grandma held up a red apple. "Will you share it with me?" she asked. Gabriel nodded. Grandma cut the apple with her safe knife. Gabriel chewed his piece slowly. It was sweet and juicy. He put the green ball next to the blue spoon and the yellow cup.

"Look, Grandma," said Gabriel. "All my colors, in a row!" Grandma laughed and took a big bite of her apple.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Eliana went to the art gallery with her grandma. Eliana wanted to paint a picture of her toy monkey. The paint corner had little pots of colour.

"I need orange," said Eliana. "My monkey has an orange tummy."

But there was no orange pot. There was red. There was yellow. There was blue. Eliana looked and looked. No orange anywhere.

Eliana picked up a brush. She put red on the paper. Then she dabbed yellow right on top of the red spot. She swirled her brush around and around.

The red spot turned orange! Eliana gasped. The paint had made a new colour, all by itself.

"Grandma, look!" said Eliana. "My monkey can have his tummy now."

She painted a big orange tummy. Then she painted a blue tail and a red hat. Her monkey looked warm in his new colours.

Eliana was thirsty after all that painting. Grandma brought her water in a small paper cup.

Eliana looked at the cup. "Yellow cup, blue water," she said. She tipped a little blue paint towards the yellow cup. Then she stopped. "Not for drinking," she told her monkey. She put the paint down and took a big sip of water instead.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: counting, comparing amounts, and shapes
fact: When you count a group of things, the last number you say tells how many there are. You get the same answer no matter which one you count first.
story:
Ethan stood at the snack table at school. There were two plates of crackers. He wanted the plate with more crackers. But which plate had more?

His teacher, Miss Kim, said, "Count them." Ethan pointed at the red plate. He counted, "One, two, three, four, five." The last number was five. Then he counted the blue plate. "One, two, three, four, five, six." The last number was six. Six was more. Ethan picked the blue plate.

His friend Milo said, "Count again. Start at the other end." Ethan watched his own finger. He started from the last cracker this time. "One, two, three, four, five." The red plate still said five. He counted the blue plate backward. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six again!

Ethan counted both plates two more times. Each way gave the same numbers. Miss Kim smiled. Milo tried counting his own crackers from both ends too.

"Naughty crackers," said Milo. "They keep moving around." But the numbers stayed the same.

Ethan took his blue plate to the little line by the window. "Six crackers," he said. "I counted them every way."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Hannah sat by the train window. She was going on a big family trip. Her bear, Mr. Buttons, sat on her lap.

"I want to see Grandma now," said Hannah. "Is the train slow today?"

Daddy looked out the window. "Rain," he said. "Lots of rain on the glass."

Hannah watched the rain. One drop slid down the window. It bumped into a little drop. Then the two drops made one big drop. The big drop slid down fast, like a race car.

Hannah gasped. She put her finger on the glass. The drop followed her finger! She moved her finger. The drop went that way too. It was a rain puppy.

"Look, Daddy!" she said. "I can lead it!"

She led the drop all the way down. Then it fell off the edge. Hannah laughed.

"Where did it go?" asked Daddy.

"It went to find Grandma," said Hannah. "It will tell her we are coming."

Then the train went around a bend. The sun came out. The rain stopped. And outside, Hannah saw one big yellow thing in a field.

"Daddy! A giant banana!"

"That is a moon bounce," said Daddy, laughing. "Maybe Grandma has one too."

"Maybe!" said Hannah. She hugged Mr. Buttons tight.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Mama lit the little lamps with a match. Eleanor watched from her chair. "Can I help?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "You can put out the flowers."

One lamp, two lamps, three lamps. They made circles of light on the table. Eleanor put a flower by each one. The lamp made the flower glow. "Mama, look! The light touches the petals!" The petals looked like fire, but soft and orange.

Then Eleanor found one lamp with no flower. "Who lives here?" she asked. "Nobody yet," said Mama. Eleanor ran to the kitchen. She came back with a marigold, a rose, and a messy handful of petals. She made a little pile, red and yellow. Papa set the lamp on top. The whole pile glowed. "More light!" said Eleanor. "More flowers!" said Mama, and she hugged her tight.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Sophie wanted a big carrot of her own. Grandma gave her three little seeds. Sophie dug a small hole in the dirt. She dropped the seeds in and patted the soil. Then she poured water from her small blue can.

The next day, nothing grew. Sophie looked and looked. "Where is my carrot?" she asked. "The seeds are still working," said Grandma. So Sophie watered the dirt each day. She pulled one tiny weed that came up close.

One morning, green leaves popped out of the soil. Sophie clapped her hands. A pig in the next pen turned its head to look. Day by day, the leaves grew tall. At last, Grandma pulled up a fat orange carrot. "Wash it first," said Grandma. The water turned muddy. Sophie took a big crunchy bite.
